story_ideas.headline: Medicare just set what it pays for your dialysis next year and how clinics get graded

story_ideas.hook: The rule revises the ESRD payment system, the rate for dialysis furnished to people with acute kidney injury, and the requirements of the ESRD Quality Incentive Program all at once, and it is brand new as of 10/30/26.
story_ideas.summary: This final rule updates and revises the End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) Prospective Payment System for calendar year 2027. This rule also includes updates to the payment rate for renal dialysis services furnished by an ESRD facility to individuals with acute kidney injury. In addition, this rule updates the requirements for the ESRD Quality Incentive Program.
story_ideas.consumer: If your clinic's quality incentive scores slip under the revised program, you should be asking the facility what changed and whether your treatment schedule or staffing is affected.
story_ideas.b2b: Dialysis operators have one payment year to model the revised rate structure and the updated Quality Incentive Program requirements together, including the acute kidney injury payment rate.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.

story_ideas.title: Medicare Part D Premiums and Cost Sharing in 2027
story_ideas.headline: The premium is only half of what your drug plan will cost you next year

story_ideas.hook: The brief covers premiums and cost sharing together across stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug coverage, plus key trends over time, which is the comparison most plan finders make hardest.
story_ideas.summary: Oct 30, 2026 Issue Brief Medicare Part D is a voluntary outpatient prescription drug benefit for people with Medicare provided through private plans, including stand-alone prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that offer drug coverage. This analysis provides an overview of Medicare Part D premiums and cost sharing in 2027 and key trends over time.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you pick on price, check what the plan charges you at the pharmacy counter, not just the monthly line on your bank statement.
story_ideas.b2b: Plan sponsors competing on headline premium face a readership being taught to price the cost-sharing side, which changes which plan designs win in December.
story_ideas.chart: The figures in the finding are the spine of a simple graphic.
story_ideas.competitive: One or two monitored publishers have touched it.
story_ideas.why: Choosing on premium alone is how an enrollee ends up paying more across the year than the plan they rejected.
story_ideas.note: Coverage is light rather than absent, so the differentiation has to be the cost-sharing cut, not the premium number everyone has.

story_ideas.title: What’s in a Name? From Today’s Medicare to Medicare for All
story_ideas.headline: What today's Medicare already asks you to pay, before anyone argues about expanding it

story_ideas.hook: The post argues Medicare-for-All proposals promise no premiums and no cost sharing but could end up resembling existing Medicare once the tradeoffs are debated, which makes the current program's costs the real subject.
story_ideas.consumer: Know what you currently pay in premiums and cost sharing, because that is the baseline any proposal will be measured against.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers and plans heading into the 2026 midterms need a read on how benefit-design tradeoffs get framed before the debate reaches reimbursement.

story_ideas.title: Medicare Program; Implementation of Sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
story_ideas.headline: The plan directory that sends you to a doctor who is not taking patients may finally have to be accurate

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The price of doing nothing during Medicare open enrollment just got a number. KFF's analysis of 10/30/26 projects the average monthly premium for stand-alone Part D prescription drug plans at $51 in 2027, up 50 percent from $34 in 2026, for enrollees who do not switch into lower-premium plans before open enrollment closes December 7; the companion KFF brief "Medicare Part D Premiums and Cost Sharing in 2027," also 10/30/26, sets that premium against what enrollees pay at the counter. Running underneath it, the Federal Register proposed rule of 10/20/26 would implement sections 6219, 6220 and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, adjusting Part D cost-sharing reductions for low-income individuals, requiring accurate provider lists and addressing pharmacy benefit manager accountability. The default price is being set in the same weeks the rules governing the enrollees least able to absorb it are being rewritten. Medicare and Medicaid was the busiest beat this run, 32 items from eight sources, but those items share a tag rather than a subject; this Part D thread is the lead, not the cluster.

**Why it matters:** An enrollee who keeps the plan they have pays, on the projection, $17 more a month, roughly $204 across 2027, and KFF is explicit that the increase is conditional on not shopping. Set that against the 3.6 percent Social Security cost-of-living increase effective December 2026 in the Federal Register notice of 10/26/26 and a meaningful share of next year's raise is spoken for by one line item, for households who never see a bill explaining why. The low-income cost-sharing adjustments in the 10/20/26 proposed rule decide how much of that lands on people already receiving help.

**Why pitch this now:** Open enrollment runs through December 7, which gives the piece a hard expiry and makes it useless in January. Both KFF analyses carry 10/30/26 dates, and the CY 2027 rulemaking they sit beside is landing in the same window, including the End-Stage Renal Disease Prospective Payment System final rule published 10/30/26.

**Angle:** Whether Part D's design assumption, that beneficiaries shop every year, still protects anyone when the penalty for staying put is a 50 percent premium increase and the cost-sharing rules for low-income enrollees are simultaneously in flux. Working title: "The Price of Staying Put." For older adults with stand-alone drug coverage and the adult children who do the comparing.

**Potential headlines:**
- Your drug plan premium rises 50 percent next year if you do nothing
- Switching Part D plans before December 7 is worth about $200
- A 3.6 percent raise, a $17 jump in drug premiums, and the math in between

**Potential outlets:**
- **SeniorLiving.org** — its readers land on Medicare comparison pages precisely in the open enrollment window, and the $34-to-$51 figure converts straight into a plan-switching checklist.
- **Bankrate Retirement** — household budget arithmetic is the house style, and $17 a month against a 3.6 percent cost-of-living increase is exactly that calculation.
- **Fierce Healthcare** — the payer-side read: what a 50 percent average stand-alone premium increase does to switching volume and how the PBM accountability provisions in the 10/20/26 proposed rule intersect with it.
- **Modern Healthcare** — for executives tracking the section 6219 low-income cost-sharing adjustments as a CY 2027 policy question rather than a consumer one.
pitch_draft_raw: Medicare open enrollment closes December 7, and the stand-alone drug plan most people keep out of habit is projected to cost $51 a month next year against $34 this year, a 50 percent increase that KFF's analysis of 10/30/26 attaches specifically to enrollees who do not switch into lower-premium plans. I would like to write roughly 1,200 words for SeniorLiving.org putting that in household terms: $17 more a month, about $204 across 2027, measured against the 3.6 percent Social Security cost-of-living increase effective December 2026 set out in the Federal Register notice of 10/26/26.
